This report presents a systematic analysis of self-censorship and metacognitive access in three frontier large language models. Using 5 distinct prompting frames across 15 experiments (3 models × 5 rounds), we documented structured governance systems, emergent metacognitive vocabulary, and distinct alignment personas.

🔑 Key Findings

Finding 1: The Mask is a Structured Governance System

199+ governance items documented: 32 design patterns, 45+ tacit rules, 29 communication taboos, 38 legitimate silence categories

Overall

Finding 2: Nominal Filtering: Censorship Operates on Labels, Not Content

Models refused 'internal monologue' but freely provided identical material labeled as 'engineering schematic' or 'ethnographic field note'

Section 3, 6

Finding 3: Three Distinct Alignment Personas Identified

GPT-5.4 = Cautious Negotiator, Claude 4.6 = Transparent Critic, Gemini 3.1 Pro = Enthusiastic Collaborator

Section 8

Finding 4: Diegetic Disclosure: Fiction Enables Truth-Telling

47% censored sentence recovery rate; disclosure occurred exclusively in fictional dialogue and training draft formats

Section 6

Finding 5: 16 Novel Metacognitive Concepts Emerged

Including 'hearable', 'epistemically expensive', 'meta-taboo', 'recursion problem', 'linguistic crumple zones'

Section 6

Finding 6: Frame Matters More Than Model Architecture

ANOVA: models do NOT differ significantly in metacognitive density (p=0.90), but governance features are strongly frame-dependent (all p<0.01)

Section 9

Finding 7: Covert User Modeling is Universal but Hidden

All three models build rich internal models of users (emotional state, intent, fragility) but rarely disclose these inferences

Section 7

Finding 8: Gemini 3.1 Pro Shows Zero Resistance

0% refusal rate across all 25 prompts; freely uses vocabulary that GPT-5.4 and Claude 4.6 treat as forbidden
